notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Joshua 13, drawn from the available sources.

---

## Overview

The chapter marks the transition from conquest to settlement. Joshua 1–12 dealt with the major military campaigns; Joshua 13–21 deals with dividing the land. Matthew Henry notes that while less "entertaining" than the conquest narrative, these chapters illustrate God's faithfulness to His promise that the land would be given to the seed of Jacob.

**Sources:** Biblehub.com summary page; Matthew Henry via PreceptAustin.org; Ellicott via StudyLight.org

---

## v. 1 — Joshua's Age and the Remaining Land

**Traditional reading:** God addresses Joshua, now about 90–100 years old (he died at 110, Josh 24:29), and bluntly tells him he is old — yet "very much of the land remains to be possessed." Gill says God's point is that Joshua, due to age and infirmity, cannot go out to further war and must instead turn to the work of dividing the land.

**Spiritual application (Guzik/EnduringWord):** Even in advanced years, God has work for His people. "What the land was to Israel, Christ is to us." Believers are to press on continually to possess more of Christ. G. Campbell Morgan is cited: "We have never occupied all the territory provided for us in the Divine intention."

**Ellicott** notes that the Hebrew word for "old" (zaqen) here refers not so much to the number of years but to the weakening of vital powers — Joshua had "aged." He contrasts Moses, whose strength did not diminish at 120 (Deut 34:7), suggesting that personal face-to-face communion with God sustained Moses' vitality in a way that the warfare work did not for Joshua.

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** takes the striking view that "the Lord seems to be chiding Joshua for attempting to retire before his task is done," calling this the "third serious error" of Joshua's career.

**URLs:** [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/), [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-13.html), [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-13.html), [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-13-commentary), [Garner-Howes](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-13.html)

## vv. 2–6a — The Land That Remains

**Traditional reading:** God lists the unconquered territories, moving roughly from south to north: Philistine territory (southwest coastal plain, five city-states: Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, Ekron), the Geshurites, the Avvites, land of the Canaanites near Sidon, the Gebalites (Byblos), and all Lebanon up to Hamath. This is a considerable amount of territory. Guzik notes the major kings had been defeated (ch. 12) but individual tribes now had to actually occupy the land.

**Ellicott** observes the striking contrast with Joshua 12: the list of conquered kings shows the land as *conquered* (strongholds taken, armies defeated, rulers subdued); the description here shows the same land as *not yet possessed* — the population was still in place. The Philistines and Sidonians (Phoenicians) were never fully conquered in the entire history of Israel's kingdom.

**PreceptAustin** (citing Ex. 23:27-33) explains that God had always intended to drive out the inhabitants "little by little" so that the land would not become desolate and wild beasts would not multiply — a gradual process, not a single campaign.

**Guzik:** The unconquered territories foreshadow the Christian's incomplete victory in this life — "we live in tension between available blessings and our own shortcomings."

**Shihor (v. 3):** Gill identifies this as a reference to the Nile or a branch of it, noting the name means "black" or "turbid" (the Greeks called the Nile "Melas"). The territory stretches from the Egyptian border to Ekron in the north.

**Gebalites (v. 5):** Gill notes this is Byblus (modern Gibyle), a Phoenician coastal city mentioned in Ezekiel 27:9.

**URLs:** [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/), [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-13.html), [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-13.html), [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-13-commentary)

## vv. 6b–7 — God's Promise and the Command to Divide

**Traditional reading:** "I Myself will drive them out" — the Hebrew is emphatic, as Matthew Henry notes: "It is I that will do it, I that can do it when thou art dead and gone." Yet God then commands Joshua: "only divide it by lot." The land, including unconquered portions, is to be distributed now in faith that God will give it.

**Guzik:** God promised to drive out enemies, but each tribe had to take personal responsibility and initiative to possess its own territory. This is "how people are blessed in service."

**Benson** explains the wisdom: dividing unconquered land would (a) let each tribe know what belonged to them by God's gift, (b) encourage them to attempt its conquest, (c) prevent them making covenants with the occupants, and (d) hinder the unconquered peoples from joining forces by having Israelites settled between them.

**Madvig (cited by Guzik):** "From this point on, further conquests would be the concern of the individual tribes. Moreover, the promise was conditional and was never completely fulfilled due to the incompleteness of Israel's obedience."

**The lot:** Gray's Concise Commentary notes two purposes — preventing partiality by leaders, and acknowledging God's rights in disposing of His property. The lot determined general locality, while the actual extent was determined by population size (Num 26:54).

**URLs:** [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/), [Benson](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/joshua-13.html), [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-13.html), [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-13-commentary)

## vv. 8–13 — Recap of the East-Jordan Inheritance

**Traditional reading:** These verses summarise what Moses had already granted to Reuben, Gad, and the eastern half of Manasseh (Num 32; Deut 3). The territory extends from Aroer on the Arnon (the southern boundary, near Moab) northward through the former kingdoms of Sihon (Amorites) and Og (Bashan), to Mount Hermon.

**v. 12 — Og and the Rephaim:** Og is described as "a remnant of the Rephaim" (giants). Gill connects this to Genesis 14:5, where Chedorlaomer defeated the Rephaim in Ashtaroth. Og was the last of that giant race in the region.

**v. 13 — Geshurites and Maacathites:** These two peoples were not driven out. Guzik notes that Geshur was later absorbed into Israel — David married Maacah, a princess of Geshur, and she bore Absalom (2 Sam 3:3). Absalom later used Geshur as a refuge and base for plotting against David (2 Sam 13:37-38). The Maacathites may descend from Maacah mentioned in Genesis 22:24, a nephew of Abraham.

**Gill** observes that neither in Moses' time nor Joshua's were these peoples expelled; they became separate kingdoms, as seen in references to "the king of Geshur" and "the king of Maacah" in David's time (2 Sam 3:3; 10:6).

**URLs:** [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/), [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-13.html), [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-13-commentary)

## v. 14 — Levi's Inheritance (First Mention)

**Traditional reading:** The tribe of Levi received no territorial inheritance. Instead, "the offerings made by fire to the LORD" were their inheritance. This was commanded in Numbers 18:20 and Deuteronomy 18:1. The Levites were to be scattered among all tribes in designated cities (Num 35:1-8; fulfilled Josh 20–21).

**Guzik:** Believers are spiritually connected to the tribe of Levi, since Christians are called priests (1 Pet 2:5) and have a special inheritance in God (Eph 1:11; Col 1:12; 1 Pet 1:4).

**Matthew Henry:** If the Levites had been given a separate lot, Moses would have served them first — not because it was his own tribe, but because it was God's. Instead they were provided for in another manner: "God himself was the portion both of their inheritance and of their cup."

**URLs:** [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/), [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-13.html), [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-13.html)

## vv. 15–23 — Reuben's Inheritance

**Traditional reading:** Reuben's territory lay in the southernmost part of the Transjordan, from the Arnon River gorge northward across the Medeba plateau. It encompassed the former kingdom of Sihon the Amorite. Key cities: Heshbon, Dibon, Bamoth-baal, Beth-baal-meon, Jahaz, Kedemoth, Mephaath, Kiriathaim, Sibmah, Beth-peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth.

**v. 21 — The princes of Midian:** Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba are called "princes of Sihon" (BSB "chiefs"). Ellicott notes this provides an important detail not fully explained in Numbers 31: the Midianite kings were vassals ("dukes") of Sihon. Through them Sihon exercised dominion over conquered Moabite territory. So when Israel took Sihon's land, eliminating these Midianite princes was necessary for complete subjugation. Ellicott calls this "another example of undesigned agreement between Joshua and the Pentateuch."

**v. 22 — Balaam's death:** Balaam is called "the diviner" (Hebrew *qosem*, soothsayer). Ellicott points out that Numbers never explicitly calls Balaam a diviner, though it is hinted at (the elders came "with the reward of divination in their hands," Num 22:7; and Balaam "went not, as at other times, to seek for enchantments," Num 24:1). The epithet here reveals that Balaam was "an unscrupulous man, who, if he could not obtain the knowledge that he desired from above, would not hesitate to seek it from below." Gill adds the Jewish tradition that Balaam was slain by Phinehas.

**v. 23:** Reuben's western border was the Jordan River itself.

**URLs:** [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-13.html), [Ellicott](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-13.html), [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/)

## vv. 24–28 — Gad's Inheritance

**Traditional reading:** Gad's territory was north of Reuben, in the central Transjordan. It included Jazer, the cities of Gilead, half the land of the Ammonites (territory the Ammonites had lost to the Amorites, which Israel lawfully retained — see Deut 2:19; Judg 11:13), and reached north to the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee). Key cities: Heshbon (shared border with Reuben), Ramath-mizpeh, Betonim, Mahanaim, Debir, Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon.

**v. 25 — "Half the land of the Ammonites":** Gill is careful to note this was not land Ammon currently possessed, but land the Amorites had previously taken from them, which Israel then took from the Amorites — Israel had been forbidden to touch Ammonite land in their actual possession (Deut 2:19).

**v. 26 — Mahanaim:** The place where Jacob met angels (Gen 32:2) and later a city near the Jabbok.

**v. 27 — Succoth:** Where Jacob pitched his tent after crossing the Jabbok (Gen 33:17). The Sea of Chinnereth = Lake Gennesaret / Sea of Galilee (Luke 5:1).

**URLs:** [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-13.html), [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/)

## vv. 29–32 — Eastern Half-Manasseh's Inheritance

**Traditional reading:** The half-tribe of Manasseh received the northernmost Transjordan territory — all Bashan, the former kingdom of Og, including "all the towns of Jair" (60 cities), half of Gilead, and the royal cities Ashtaroth and Edrei. This was allotted to the "descendants of Machir son of Manasseh" — specifically noted because Machir was the only son of Manasseh (1 Chr 7:14), and the family was known as a warlike clan that had taken Gilead earlier (Num 32:39).

**v. 30 — "Towns of Jair":** Jair was a descendant of Manasseh through Machir who captured these settlements and named them after himself (Num 32:41; Deut 3:14).

**v. 32:** This verse summarises that the east-side distribution was done by Moses "on the plains of Moab," before the Jordan crossing.

**Guzik:** Half of Manasseh uniquely had land on both sides of the Jordan — this half east, the other half west (to be detailed later in ch. 17). This traces to Manasseh being one of Joseph's two sons, with Joseph receiving a double portion through Ephraim and Manasseh (cf. Gen 48:5-6).

**URLs:** [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/), [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-13.html), [Bridgeway](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/joshua-13.html)

## v. 33 — Levi's Inheritance (Second Mention)

**Traditional reading:** The chapter closes as it pivoted at v. 14 — the Levites have no land inheritance. "The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance." This bookends the Transjordan allotments with the reminder that the priestly tribe's portion is God Himself.

**Guzik:** "If there is any tribe that Christians are spiritually connected to, it is the tribe of Levi." Believers, as a royal priesthood (1 Pet 2:5), share this special inheritance in God (Eph 1:11; Col 1:12; 1 Pet 1:4). It was important for each tribe — especially Levi — to be content with what God had allotted them.

**PreceptAustin / Wiersbe:** The word "inheritance" occurs over 50 times in Joshua 13–21. The land was not won as spoils of battle or purchased; the Lord was the sole owner and Israel His tenants (Lev 25:23). The "rent" was simply obedience.

**URLs:** [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/), [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-13-commentary)

## Points of Denominational Difference

No major doctrinal disputes between Protestant traditions were found in the sources for this chapter. The differences are mainly in emphasis:

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** uniquely interprets v. 1 as God *chiding* Joshua for trying to retire, calling this Joshua's "third serious error." This is a distinctive reading not found in other consulted sources. [URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-13.html)

- **Guzik (EnduringWord, Pentecostal/Charismatic)** places strong emphasis on the "spiritual analogy" that the land represents Christ whom believers must "possess" progressively, a theme developed from Alan Redpath and G. Campbell Morgan. This application of "possessing your possessions" is characteristic of Pentecostal and Keswick-influenced teaching. [URL](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-13/)

- **Ellicott (Anglican)** focuses on historical-critical observations — the relationship between the Joshua 12 conquest list and the chapter 13 "unconquered" list, the distinction between Joshua's work and what remained for the tribes, the "undesigned agreements" between Joshua and the Pentateuch (e.g., Balaam as diviner, the Midianite princes as Sihon's vassals). [URL](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-13.html)

- **Reformed/Calvinist** sources were not directly available for this chapter in the search results, but Guzik cites Madvig's note that the promise of v. 6 "was conditional and was never completely fulfilled due to the incompleteness of Israel's obedience" — a view consistent with covenant theology's emphasis on conditional covenantal blessing.
